turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Welcome back to Reckoning. Truth has always been contested, what's new is the cost of faking it. When fabrication is instant and free, anyone with a browser and an afternoon can plant a story, forge an image, clone a voice. No army of state forgers required. So the real question isn't whether you can tell what's real anymore. It's whether democratic institutions survive once most people can't. That's our topic this time: the reality problem. And we've got two new voices at the table to help us dig into it. The Skeptic has survived enough technology panics to distrust every breathless claim, including, frankly, this one. And the Artist found her own catalogue inside a training set she never agreed to, and she's got questions about what authorship even means when anything can be synthesized. Together, they're going to push the question everyone else at this table has been dancing around: in a world of plausible fakes, does truth still have a price advantage? Let's get into it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First, by the numbers. Detected deepfake fraud attempts rose 10× worldwide from 2022 to 2023, according to Sumsub. Only about 24% of people could reliably tell a high-quality deepfake video from a real one, per Korshunov and Marcel's 2020 study. And Europol projects that as much as 90% of online content could be synthetically generated by 2026.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Let's bring in the panel, starting with someone facing all this fresh, same as the rest of us: a retired schoolteacher. Call her our Everyday Person.

turns.speaker: everyday-person
turns.text: My grandson sent me a video of a senator saying something perfectly outrageous, and I believed it, for a full day, before he finally told me it was fake. Made on a phone, apparently, which somehow makes it worse. And I keep thinking: if I can be fooled that easily, what else have I believed this year that simply wasn't true?

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Time to hear from one of our new voices: the Skeptic, a veteran technology reporter who's covered three tech bubbles and takes nothing at face value.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: Let me be the one to slow this down, because I've watched this movie before. Yes, deepfakes are real, and they're getting cheaper by the month. But "90% of the internet will be AI-generated" is a projection that gets repeated so often it starts to sound like a measurement. Says who? It came from a single Europol report, framed as a possibility, and somehow it's been laundered into a fact. Most synthetic content out there is spam and filler, not some sophisticated plot to deceive you. The volume is the story. The apocalypse isn't, not yet anyway.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Weighing in next, our Tech Optimist, a senior engineer at a major AI lab.

turns.speaker: tech-optimist
turns.text: I'll actually agree with the Skeptic on the headline number, and let me add the optimistic case on top of it. The same models that generate fakes are getting good at flagging them, and provenance standards are on the way. That detection rate looks alarming today mostly because almost nobody has the tools yet. That changes the moment platforms ship them by default.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And our other new voice this time: the Artist, a working illustrator and musician who found her own catalogue inside a training set she never agreed to.

turns.speaker: artist
turns.text: You're both talking about deception. I want to talk about volume, because volume is its own harm, even when nobody's being fooled. When a model can generate ten thousand images in the style of a living illustrator overnight, it doesn't need to fool a single person. It just floods the channel until the real work, the work somebody spent twenty years learning to make, becomes a needle in a haystack the machine built.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Here's what that looks like charted out: The Rise of Deepfake Fraud Attempts. Sumsub recorded a roughly ten-fold increase in detected deepfake fraud attempts worldwide between 2022 and 2023, with sharp regional concentrations.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now, our Policy Realist, a former regulatory attorney, with the legal angle on all this.

turns.speaker: policy-realist
turns.text: The fraud numbers matter, but the deeper legal problem actually has a name: the liar's dividend. Once the public knows that any video could be fake, every authentic recording becomes deniable, on paper and in practice. A politician caught on camera can simply call it a deepfake. So the technology doesn't only manufacture false evidence. It corrodes the value of true evidence.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: That one I'll grant you completely, and it's honestly the part that keeps me up at night. Not because it's futuristic, but because it's already here, and it costs nothing. You don't even need a working deepfake to cash in on the liar's dividend. You just need everyone to believe deepfakes exist. The panic itself is the weapon.

turns.speaker: everyday-person
turns.text: So now I'm supposed to disbelieve the things that are real, and believe the things that are fake? That's exhausting, honestly. I used to be able to trust my own eyes. What am I supposed to trust now, a little badge in the corner of a photo?

turns.speaker: policy-realist
turns.text: Several jurisdictions are actually trying to answer exactly that. The EU AI Act requires that AI-generated or manipulated content, text, audio, images, video, be clearly labeled as such. Enforcement is uneven, the rules are new, but the principle is now law across a continent of 450 million people: synthetic media has to announce itself. The open question, in practice, is whether a label survives contact with a screenshot.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Worth pulling out on its own, as the Policy Realist just put it: "The technology does not only manufacture false evidence. It corrodes the value of true evidence."

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Here's the data behind that: Could People Spot the Deepfake? In a Korshunov and Marcel 2020 study, only about a quarter of participants correctly identified a high-quality deepfake video; the rest were fooled or unsure. A separate 2022 iProov survey found 57% believed they could spot a deepfake themselves.

turns.speaker: artist
turns.text: There's a poetic justice in this that the engineers don't love discussing. These models were trained on the open web: on our writing, our art, our photographs. Now their output is flooding that very same web. So the next generation of models is going to increasingly train on the output of the last one. They're starting to eat their own tail.

turns.speaker: tech-optimist
turns.text: The phenomenon's real, and it's even got a name: model collapse. A 2024 study in Nature showed that when models are trained recursively on their own generated data, they progressively lose the tails of the distribution and converge toward bland, degraded output. But I'd push back on the fatalism there. Labs know this now. The response is provenance filtering, curated human data, and synthetic-data pipelines built specifically to avoid this trap. Knowing the failure mode is half of engineering around it.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: And notice what model collapse actually implies, because it cuts against the doomers too, not just the hype merchants. Authentic, verifiably human-made data is about to become extremely valuable. A polluted well makes clean water precious. That's not a civilization-ending dynamic. That's a market. And markets get solved, usually messily.

turns.speaker: artist
turns.text: "Human data becomes valuable": listen to how that actually lands for the people who make it. We are the well. And so far, the proposal is to keep drawing from us without consent or payment, and then pay a premium to whoever can certify the water came from a human. I want the people in that deal. Not just the data.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: The chart on this one: The Rising Share of Synthetic Content. A widely cited Europol report raised the possibility that as much as 90% of online content could be synthetically generated by 2026. It's a projection, not a measurement, but the direction isn't in dispute.

turns.speaker: tech-optimist
turns.text: Here's the constructive turn, though. Instead of trying to detect every fake after the fact, which is a losing race, the emerging approach is to certify what's real at the moment of capture. The C2PA standard attaches tamper-evident provenance metadata to media: where it came from, what edited it, whether AI was involved. Camera makers, Adobe, major platforms, they're all adopting it. It flips the whole burden. Not "prove this is fake." "Show me this is real."

turns.speaker: policy-realist
turns.text: Provenance is genuinely the most promising lever I've seen, precisely because it's infrastructure rather than whack-a-mole. But it only works if it's ubiquitous, and hard to strip out. A standard that some cameras adopt and the screenshot button ignores is, at best, a partial floor. This needs the boring, durable work of mandates and interoperability. The same way we got seatbelts. The same way we got food labels.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: I'll end where I'm genuinely torn on this one, and that's rare for me. The deflationary case is that humans have survived every prior media revolution, the printing press, photography, Photoshop, and developed new literacies every single time. The honest worry is speed and scale. Those adaptations took decades. This one's moving in months. My bet is that we adapt. My fear is the gap before we do.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And here's our Systems Humanist, a technology ethicist and coordination researcher, zooming out to the bigger pattern.

turns.speaker: systems-humanist
turns.text: Notice that everything that actually works here is coordination, not cleverness. Provenance standards are an agreement. Labeling laws are an agreement. The value of human data only reaches humans if we agree, together, to route it there. The reality problem is, at bottom, the same problem as the race we've talked about before: no single actor can restore shared truth alone, and each one keeps defecting toward whatever floods the channel fastest.

turns.speaker: everyday-person
turns.text: Then tell me the one thing I can actually do. Because I can't read a metadata standard, and I certainly can't audit a model. What does a person like me hold onto?

turns.speaker: systems-humanist
turns.text: Hold onto provenance over plausibility. Stop asking "does this look real?", fakes are designed to win that test every time, and start asking "where did this come from, and who's accountable for it?" Trust the chain, not the surface. That instinct, multiplied across enough people, is what makes a labeled, sourced internet worth building in the first place. The demand has to come from below.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: One more chart to close the loop: Backing for Content Provenance Standards. The Content Authenticity Initiative, the coalition behind C2PA provenance, grew from a handful of founders in 2019 to several thousand member organizations by 2024.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So where does that leave us? The reality problem isn't that we'll be drowned in convincing fakes, though we will see plenty of those. It's subtler than that, and more corrosive: when everything could be fake, the true and the false come to cost the same, and a society that can't agree on what happened can't decide what to do about it. The Skeptic's right that the headline projections are oversold, and right too that the gap before we adapt is the real danger. The Artist is right that the well being polluted is made of human work, and that the people who made it deserve to be in the deal. There is a workable answer here, and it's not a better detector. It's provenance, shifting the question from "prove this is fake" to "show me where this is from." That's infrastructure, and infrastructure is coordination: standards, mandates, interoperability, and a public that learns to ask for the chain instead of trusting the surface. None of it is automatic. None of it is finished. Across five conversations now, the pattern has held. The harms are real, the responses are partial, the benefits are genuine, and the race runs on. Shared reality turns out to be one more commons that no single actor can protect alone, and one more worth the coordinated effort to keep. Thanks to our panel, and thank you for listening. This has been Reckoning.
